= Native Fetch decode admission

For an accounted native client, raw and Xerial Snappy Fetch output is admitted against the actual client's shared NativeByteAccount before output allocation.
The output owner retains its prefix and exact physical byte capacity until final native destruction.
The bundled Snappy decoder uses stack decode state, without a separate heap decode context.
Clients without an account use the original decoder and allocation paths.
Gzip, LZ4 and Zstd remain outside this cohort.

The broker actor remains the sole writer of its MessageSet reader transient.
The reader takes admission authority from its actual client, so nested Snappy remains accounted even when its immediate input is an unaccounted outer-codec shadow.
The passive output owner stores only its account pointer and immutable physical charge.
The existing native client and SDK queue/event owners retain the account monitor through native final release.
No new actor, callback lifetime, queue or waiter is introduced.

Raw Snappy validates its decoded-length header, admits output, validates the payload and only then demands shadow metadata.
Xerial detection retains the pinned strict input-length test, eight-byte magic match and ignored version/compatibility fields.
Its first pass checks each chunk's length prefix, decoded-length header and complete framing, then admits the aggregate output.
Its second pass validates and decodes chunk bodies in encounter order.
Checked output sums reject arithmetic overflow as a resource error.
A valid decoded-length header can therefore demand output before a later invalid body is discovered.
Framed empty aggregate output retains its original bad-compression result, while valid empty raw output retains a charged prefix.

Only after successful decompression does the private shadow constructor admit its native buffer root and one aligned segment header.
It uses a preallocated segment and does not enter RdBuf's fallback allocation path.
A failed root or segment malloc releases the metadata charge and leaves output ownership with the caller for cleanup.
A successful shadow installs the fixed output finalizer and the existing native refcount.
Every referring Fetch op keeps that shadow alive.
Output is freed before its charge is returned; segment and native buffer storage are freed before the final metadata charge is returned.
The last referencing native event determines release, rather than the end of the decode call.
RetainedConsumerMessage retains its event and originating consumer through the same lifetime.

Admission denial, checked allocation-size overflow and fallible output or shadow allocation failure return CRIT_SYS_RESOURCE through the existing decompression error op.
Invalid framing or payload returns BAD_COMPRESSION.
The existing MessageSet reader preserves earlier good messages and concatenates its message/error queue to the partition queue.
Only good Fetch ops determine its last accepted message offset, and the failed batch does not take its success-only next-offset update.
Earlier successful batches keep their prior updates.
The Fetch handler applies its existing partition backoff; no new fatal flag, retry guarantee or rollback is added.
The existing error-op and diagnostic-string allocations themselves still require separate admission.

The unexecuted native regression sources cover exact, one-byte-short, zero and overflow output geometry, output and both shadow malloc failures, shared Fetch-op final ownership, raw length/body demand, Xerial chunk/trailing/empty demand and comparison with the original decoder.
Public mock-cluster sources cover actual retained Snappy Fetch output and resource denial after an accepted prefix without advancing the failed offset or setting native fatal state.
All existing native and SDK test/assertion sources remain unchanged apart from additive unit registration.
These fixtures have not been compiled or run in Phase 1.

The active stock Connect account shares this bounded Snappy storage with its existing native owners.
Its finite ceiling can reject an expansion even when the compressed wire response fits receive.message.max.bytes.
The capacity policy is not a guarantee that every expansion fits.
Gzip's two-pass output and zlib internals, LZ4's context and retained growth capacity, Zstd's candidate buffers and internals, individual Fetch/error ops and strings, native client/queue/thread construction, plugins, allocator overhead and whole-native bounds remain separate obligations.
Runtime and Phase 2 gates remain open.
